title: Optimal \(\ell_1\) distortion of planar Earth Mover Distance
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors as \(n\to\infty\), the least distortion \(D(n)\) of a bi-Lipschitz embedding into \(\ell_1\) of all probability measures on the planar grid \(X_n=\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}^2\), equipped with Euclidean Earth Mover Distance. This asymptotic target was resolved in 2026: \(D(n)=\Theta(\log n)\).
why: The result identifies the optimal loss when representing planar transport by coordinatewise absolute differences. It closes a longstanding metric-embedding gap relevant to image comparison and nearest-neighbor methods, and shows that the logarithmic loss of classical representations is inherent. The completed result belongs in the historical archive rather than the active open benchmark.
status_note: Resolved: the published Gartland–Ostrovskii STOC 2026 theorem supplies the matching logarithmic lower bound. Model correspondence was checked on 13 September 2026, including Euclidean versus Manhattan ground distances and the target-space convention. This does not claim a completed Lean proof.

sentences: Planar Earth Mover Distance measures the minimum cost of transporting unit mass between two distributions on a grid.
The historical question asks for the asymptotically optimal distortion of a single embedding of the entire distribution space into ℓ1.
Naor and Schechtman left a gap between square-root-logarithmic and logarithmic distortion in the grid side length.
Gartland and Ostrovskii closed this gap with a logarithmic lower bound published at STOC 2026.
The completed record explains why the result applies to the Euclidean grid and is retained in the archive as a resolved transport-embedding problem.

definitions:
For \(n\geq2\), a probability measure is a vector \(\mu:X_n	o[0,1]\) with \(\sum_x\mu(x)=1\); all real weights are allowed. For two such vectors put \[W_n(\mu,
u)=\min_\pi\sum_{x,y\in X_n}\|x-y\|_2\pi(x,y),\] where \(\pi(x,y)\geq0\), \(\sum_y\pi(x,y)=\mu(x)\) for each \(x\), and \(\sum_x\pi(x,y)=
u(y)\) for each \(y\). The minimum exists because the set of transport plans is a nonempty compact polytope. Thus unit total mass is transported, with cost equal to distance rather than squared distance. The space \(\ell_1\) consists of real sequences \(z=(z_i)_{i\geq1}\) with \(\sum_i|z_i|<\infty\), and norm \(\|z\|_1=\sum_i|z_i|\). Define \(D(n)\) to be the infimum of all \(D\geq1\) for which a single map \(F\) from the whole probability simplex on \(X_n\) into \(\ell_1\) satisfies \(W_n(\mu,
u)\leq\|F(\mu)-F(
u)\|_1\leq D W_n(\mu,
u)\) for every pair \(\mu,
u\). Allow arbitrary nonlinear maps; the lower inequality normalizes scale and ensures injectivity. No restriction to distributions of bounded support size, uniform weights or a fixed denominator is imposed. No linearity, sketch length, algorithmic runtime or finite output dimension is required. Finite-dimensional \(\ell_1\) maps remain admissible by padding with zeros. The infimum need not be attained; matching constant-factor bounds do not require an optimum-achieving map. If no finite-distortion map exists, the infimum is infinity, although the cited upper bound rules this out for each finite grid.
answer_criterion: The original asymptotic criterion is a complete Lean-checked proof of upper and lower bounds of the same order with constants independent of \(n\). The published answer is \(\Theta(\log n)\), and proving that answer in Lean would meet the criterion. This record does not claim an existing Lean formalization. A result for one pair of distributions, only linear maps without a valid reduction, or only fixed-mass integer multisets would not suffice for the stated target.

context_blocks.text: Naor and Schechtman establish the historical gap between an \(\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})\) lower bound and an \(O(\log n)\) upper bound. The inherited card asks for the optimal dependence on grid size, not whether constant distortion is possible; the latter was already ruled out by their result.

Gartland and Ostrovskii’s STOC 2026 paper closes that gap: Theorem 1.1 gives \(\Theta(\log n)\) distortion for the transportation-cost space of the planar grid. Their reduction to linear maps identifies its distortion with that of the Earth Mover space of probability measures.

The 2026 grid theorem uses the shortest-path grid metric, which is the planar Manhattan metric. On the same vertices, Euclidean distance is between \(1/\sqrt2\) times that metric and that metric. The corresponding transport distances satisfy the same comparison, so the logarithmic order transfers to the Euclidean ground metric here.

The lower bound is proved even for embeddings into the larger Lebesgue space \(L_1\), so it also applies to \(\ell_1\). The historical upper-bound constructions can be realized with finitely many \(\ell_1\) coordinates for each finite grid. The target-space notation therefore does not leave an asymptotic gap in this card.

A separate 2026 paper by Gartland, Ostrovskii, Rabani and Young extends the sharp dependence to higher-dimensional grids with dimension-uniform constants. Its planar case explicitly relies on the Gartland–Ostrovskii theorem. It is supporting later context, not the sole basis for identifying a planar resolution.

Grid side length and the number of grid vertices differ by a square, which changes a logarithm only by a constant factor. The number of support points of an individual distribution is a different parameter and is not substituted for grid size. Sketching independently represented point sets is likewise a separate computational question.
